strengths: The paper introduces a clean and intuitive adaptation of test-time training (TTT) to the protein domain by leveraging masked language modeling pre-training directly on single test sequences without needing external data or MSAs.
Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning three major tasks in protein machine learning: zero-shot fitness prediction, structure prediction (protein folding), and protein function classification.
The method demonstrates consistent improvements across multiple architectures and scales, including ESM2, SaProt, ESMFold, and ESM3, achieving competitive/state-of-the-art results on ProteinGym.

The paper provides insightful analysis linking test-time adaptation to perplexity minimization and establishes a well-constructed validation split from MaveDB to ensure unbiased hyperparameter tuning.
The manuscript is clearly written, well-organized, and provides thorough implementation details and ablation studies in the appendix.
weaknesses: The evaluation on protein structure prediction is restricted to a very small subset of 18 targets in CAMEO selected post-hoc based on low pLDDT (<70) and high perplexity (>=6). It remains unclear whether TTT maintains performance or degrades quality when applied to the full, uncurated CAMEO benchmark.
For the largest models (e.g., SaProt 650M on ProteinGym), the absolute improvement from TTT is relatively modest (from 0.4569 to 0.4583), despite substantial computational cost.

Test-time optimization introduces non-trivial inference latency (e.g., ESM3 inference time increasing from ~1s to ~20s per sequence), particularly when selecting the optimal stopping step requires evaluating the downstream folding module at each step.

strengths: Conceptual clarity and motivation: Adapting test-time training (TTT) via masked language modeling to single protein sequences is well-motivated, conceptually clean, and directly bridges self-supervised pre-training objectives with downstream test inference.

Comprehensive cross-task evaluation: The method is validated across three central tasks in protein machine learning—fitness prediction (ProteinGym), structure prediction (ESMFold and ESM3), and function classification (TPS substrate and subcellular localization)—demonstrating broad applicability across varied head architectures (log-odds, random forest, attention, and geometric decoders).

Insightful analysis of mechanisms: The connection drawn between TTT, pseudo-perplexity minimization, and performance gains is insightful, supported by empirical analyses showing that TTT provides the most substantial benefits on challenging proteins with low MSA depth.

Methodological rigor in hyperparameter selection: The authors curate a separate validation set from MaveDB to tune hyperparameters for zero-shot fitness prediction, avoiding contamination on the ProteinGym benchmark.
weaknesses: Modest effect sizes on larger models: While gains are noticeable on smaller models (e.g., ESM2 35M), the improvements on the strongest 650M parameter fitness models are marginal (e.g., SaProt 650M improves from 0.4569 to 0.4583 on ProteinGym, and shows zero improvement on MaveDB in Table 6). Similarly, function prediction metrics exhibit very slight improvements (e.g., +0.006 mAP for TPS and +0.007 accuracy for localization).

Selective evaluation on structure prediction: The structure prediction benchmark is filtered down to a very small set of 18 'challenging' targets out of 194 in CAMEO. It remains unclear what effect TTT has when applied to the full, uncurated CAMEO test set—specifically whether it causes regression or stability issues on non-challenging targets.

Test-time computational footprint: While LoRA and gradient accumulation make single-target TTT technically feasible on a single GPU, the test-time overhead (e.g., 20–30s per protein) poses a bottleneck for high-throughput screening applications where thousands or millions of variants need evaluation.

Step selection and sensitivity to overfitting: While structure prediction benefits from an intrinsic confidence metric (pLDDT) for step selection, fitness and function prediction rely on a fixed step count chosen globally on a validation set. As Figure 11 illustrates, fine-tuning on a single sequence carries a significant risk of rapid overfitting if the step budget or learning rate is miscalibrated for an outlier protein.

strengths: Intuitive and unified framework: The paper presents a straightforward adaptation of test-time training (TTT) to protein language models, leveraging the pre-existing masked language modeling (MLM) head within standard Y-shaped architectures without needing external homologous sequences or MSAs.

Broad scope of tasks: The authors validate the method across diverse biological downstream problems, including zero-shot mutation fitness estimation, 3D structure prediction, and enzyme/subcellular function classification.

Grounding in perplexity minimization: Connecting TTT updates directly to sequence pseudo-perplexity provides an interpretable conceptual justification for why representation refinement occurs on single targets.
weaknesses: Marginal empirical gains on large models and function tasks: The reported performance improvements on competitive models are extremely small. On ProteinGym with 650M-parameter models (both ESM2 and SaProt), the gain in average Spearman correlation is merely +0.0014 (e.g., SaProt 650M increases from 0.4569 to 0.4583), which is practically negligible despite the claim of setting a new state of the art. Similarly, function prediction improvements in Table 3 are within fractions of a percent or marginal confidence intervals (e.g., TPS substrate mAP increases by 0.006, subcellular localization accuracy by 0.007).

Severe selection bias in structure prediction evaluation: In Section 4.2 and Table 2, the CAMEO evaluation is restricted to an arbitrary subset of only 18 'challenging' targets (filtered by ESMFold pLDDT < 70 and perplexity >= 6) out of the 194 test targets. Omitting the evaluation on the full uncurated CAMEO benchmark obscures whether TTT degrades performance or destabilizes predictions on average- or high-confidence proteins.

Significant computational overhead at inference time: TTT requires performing multiple forward and backward passes (30 to 50 optimization steps) per individual test sequence. As illustrated in Figure 7, ESM3 inference latency increases roughly 20-fold (from 1 second to ~20 seconds per target). For high-throughput applications, directed evolution screening, or proteome-scale analysis, this creates an impractical computational bottleneck.

Lack of reliable test-time stopping criteria: While structure prediction can exploit pLDDT as an internal confidence proxy to halt training, fitness and function prediction tasks lack an instance-level stopping metric. Figure 11 clearly shows that TTT rapidly overfits to the test sequence when hyperparameters or step counts deviate, making practical deployment fragile without ground-truth feedback.

Limited methodological novelty: Adapting backbones at test time via self-supervised masked reconstruction objectives is an established technique directly imported from computer vision (e.g., Gandelsman et al., 2022) to protein masked language models.

strengths: Compelling adaptation of the test-time training (TTT) paradigm to protein language models (PLMs), leveraging masked language modeling to reduce sequence perplexity on-the-fly without needing labeled test data.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning three major computational biology tasks: 3D structure prediction (CAMEO), zero-shot fitness prediction (ProteinGym and a newly curated MaveDB benchmark), and function prediction (terpene synthase classification and subcellular localization).
Evaluated across diverse model families (ESM2, ESMFold, ESM3, HelixFold-Single, SaProt, ProSST, MSA Transformer) and model sizes ranging from 35M to 3B parameters.

Convincing real-world case studies demonstrating practical utility on difficult biological targets: improving antibody CDR loop modeling on SAbDab and enhancing 19% of low-confidence viral structures in the Big Fantastic Virus Database (BFVD).

Thorough investigation of optimization details, including the use of LoRA for parameter-efficient adaptation of large models (3B ESM2 backbone), SGD for stable test-time dynamics, and pLDDT as an unsupervised confidence metric to mitigate overfitting.
weaknesses: Structure prediction evaluation on CAMEO is restricted to a small subset of 18 targets filtered by low pLDDT and high perplexity; reporting results across the entire uncurated CAMEO test set (194 targets) would demonstrate whether applying ProteinTTT universally causes regressions on already well-predicted proteins.

On the zero-shot ProteinGym benchmark, the performance improvements for larger models are statistically significant but modest in absolute magnitude (e.g., +0.0014 for ESM2-650M and SaProt-650M, +0.0019 for ProSST).

Computational overhead at inference time is notable compared to base feedforward inference (ESMFold inference increases from ~2s to ~46s per target), which may limit applicability in high-throughput proteome-scale screening.
Minor editorial oversights: Figure A11 still refers to an earlier internal working name ('ProteinPin') instead of 'ProteinTTT'.

strengths: Conceptual novelty: The paper successfully adapts the test-time training (TTT) paradigm to protein language models (PLMs), presenting a clean, self-supervised mechanism to customize models to individual sequences or multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) on the fly.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The method is validated across diverse downstream tasks and well-established models, including structure prediction (ESMFold, ESM3, HelixFold-Single), zero-shot fitness prediction (ESM2, SaProt, ProSST, MSA Transformer), and function prediction (EnzymeExplorer, Light Attention).

Compelling case studies: The practical utility of the approach is convincingly illustrated on real-world, high-impact biological challenges, notably antibody CDR loop modeling on SAbDab and the expansion of high-confidence viral structure predictions in BFVD.

Thorough methodological analysis and implementation: The paper provides clear justifications linking MLM loss minimization to perplexity reduction, uses LoRA and SGD to enable single-GPU execution with reasonable runtime overhead, and provides extensive validation studies and ablations in the appendix.
weaknesses: Selective evaluation in structure prediction: The benchmark on CAMEO is evaluated exclusively on a filtered subset of 18 low-confidence targets (pLDDT < 70, perplexity >= 6). While addressing hard targets is well-motivated, it remains important to report performance across the full, unfiltered CAMEO test set to verify that test-time adaptation does not degrade high-confidence or in-distribution predictions.

Modest absolute gains on large-scale fitness models: While improvements on smaller models (e.g., ESM2-35M) are substantial, the absolute gains on state-of-the-art larger models (such as ESM2-650M, SaProt-650M, and ProSST-2048) are relatively modest (e.g., +0.0014 to +0.0019 in average Spearman correlation).

Inference latency overhead: Test-time optimization requires multiple forward/backward passes and gradient updates (e.g., increasing ESMFold inference time from ~2s to ~46s per target). While acceptable for single-protein wet-lab workflows, this limits scalability for high-throughput or proteome-wide screening.

Dependence on confidence metrics for early stopping: The optimal stopping point heavily relies on output confidence metrics such as pLDDT for structure prediction. For tasks lacking well-calibrated confidence estimators (e.g., fitness prediction), the method relies on fixed step counts, which can risk overfitting if learning rates and accumulation steps are not properly tuned.

strengths: Novel conceptual adaptation: Adapting the test-time training (TTT) paradigm to protein language models via self-supervised masked language modeling is intuitive, well-motivated, and directly addresses the practical biology use-case where researchers focus on single, difficult protein targets.

Broad empirical evaluation: The paper demonstrates the applicability of ProteinTTT across three fundamental protein tasks (structure prediction, zero-shot mutation fitness prediction, and function classification) across diverse model families and scales (ESM2, ESM3, HelixFold-Single, SaProt, ProSST, MSA Transformer).

High-impact case studies: The practical utility is compellingly demonstrated on real-world challenges where standard models struggle, specifically antibody CDR loop modeling on SAbDab and viral protein structure prediction on the Big Fantastic Virus Database (BFVD).

Thoughtful engineering: The inclusion of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA), gradient accumulation, and confidence-based early stopping (e.g., using pLDDT) makes per-sequence optimization computationally feasible on standard hardware (single A100 GPU).
weaknesses: Selective evaluation on structure prediction: The structure prediction benchmark on CAMEO is evaluated only on a heavily filtered subset of 18 low-confidence targets (pLDDT < 70, perplexity >= 6). While targeting hard cases is sensible, it remains unclear whether applying ProteinTTT uniformly across average or high-confidence targets preserves performance or induces degradation/overfitting.

Marginal numerical gains on large fitness models: While the gains are consistent, the absolute improvements on full-scale fitness benchmarks for larger models are modest (e.g., ESM2-650M increases from 0.4139 to 0.4153, and ProSST increases from 0.5068 to 0.5087 on ProteinGym), suggesting diminishing returns as the underlying model capacity grows.

Inference latency overhead: Test-time optimization requires dozens of backward passes per sequence, increasing inference latency considerably (e.g., from ~2s to ~46s for ESMFold). Although still faster than AlphaFold2 MSA generation, this poses a bottleneck for proteome-scale high-throughput screening.

Heuristic stopping criteria outside structure prediction: While structure prediction benefits from an intrinsic confidence score (pLDDT) to select the best checkpoint, tasks like fitness prediction lack a sequence-level confidence function, relying on a fixed step count that may be sensitive to overfitting depending on sequence length and complexity.
Minor presentation slip: Figure A11 still contains references to an internal/working name ('ProteinPin') on the y-axis and legend rather than ProteinTTT.
